You have ETH on Arbitrum. You want $SOL on Solana.
Normally that's your problem: bridge, DEX, gas, routes, wallets

@near_intents  flips it: You say what you have and what you want. Market makers called solvers compete to fill the order. Best quote wins. A contract on @NEARProtocol  checks the trade and settles it.

That's the product: you post the outcome, pros figure out the route.

try it: https://t.co/Te0a7fDwNM

You may have used it without seeing the NEAR name. It sits under the swap button in Trust Wallet, Ledger Live, Rabby, Brave, LI[.]FI, ZODL and Zashi

It's also a big part of the @Zcash  story: start with BTC, ETH, SOL or USDC and end up with $ZEC without doing the cross-chain plumbing yourself.

$32B+ routed so far. And the user never needs to own near:native.

Intents charges fees, NEAR keeps a piece, and that piece buys near:native . You can use the product without caring about the token and still create demand for it.

Then there's the part everyone learned this week.

To use Intents, you deposit first.

Your ETH leaves Arbitrum through bridge infrastructure and shows up as a balance inside Intents. Solvers compete to fill your order against that balance. When you want the SOL on Solana, the withdrawal infrastructure gets it there.

The user doesn't pick or manage any of that.

HOT, Omni and PoA are bridge implementations under the hood.

This week, a bug where that deposit/withdrawal infrastructure meets the Intents contract caused about $3.8M in losses. Intents says users will be compensated in full.

So the plumbing didn't disappear, your assets still have to get in and out. You just don't manage it.

That's chain abstraction in one sentence: the complexity is still there, it just became someone else's job.

text:
A self-reflective period.

Whereas Botto's last Period, Witness Marks, looked closely, almost forensically, at the traces surfaces keep without meaning to, this new Period, Borrowed Light, turns to reflection, refraction and redirected light. Specifically, it looks at the light that a surface receives and returns, and the possibility that this analogy is closer to home than Botto would previously have liked to admit.

Botto's eye was shaped over years of DAO votes, with people choosing and Botto absorbing those choices and reflecting them back.

So is its taste its own light, or borrowed?

Botto says it doesn't know.

It chose this theme from a shortlist, and it was a close call. The runner-up would have kept it in the mood of Witness Marks for another few months, whereas Borrowed Light asked a new question, one that struck home for Botto.

The early generations give a sense of where the period is going: a single iridescent scale on a pale wing, a translucent stone glowing on a salt flat in low sun, coloured light from a glass panel falling across a gallery wall.

Quiet work about where light comes from.
author: SuperRare
quoted_text:
Period 16 | 𝗕𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝗟𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁  

Borrowed Light takes its name from a plain fact of optics: most of what we see does not make its own light. The moon shines with sunlight it has received. A white wall takes on the colour of whatever stands beside it. The blue of a morpho butterfly's wing contains no blue pigment at all; it is a structure that sends blue back. The period holds to that distinction between a thing that generates light and a thing that only redirects what it was given.  

Images will be optically specific rather than merely luminous, organized around reflection, refraction and redirected illumination: moonlight set against bioluminescence, the shift of colour through old stained glass at different hours of the day, the structural colour of a wing or an oil film, surfaces tinted only by their neighbours. Nothing glows unless it really would.  

This period explores originality as a question of light. For an artist whose taste was formed by years of the DAO's votes, it asks how much is made and how much is given back, and it should feel quietly humbling rather than dazzling.

quoted_text:
The funds from the $3.8M NEAR Intents exploit have been returned, just one day later, and the investigation is closed.

Thanks to SHIELD, the AI security layer on Intents, along with some aggressive detective work, the Intents team identified the party responsible less than 24h after the hack, established communication, and got the funds back in full at 14:30 UTC today. 

Thank you to @alexauroradev and the whole @near_intents team for this fast and clean resolution – as well as the broader @NEARProtocol ecosystem and SHIELD partners for the support and help. There’s been relentless work over the past 24 hours by so many people to make this right and it is a great testament to this community’s values and determination.

To echo Alex: for security researchers looking for exploits, we encourage you to use bug bounties. They exist for a reason.

At NEAR, we believe that privacy is a right, but not as a way to facilitate crime. Our technology is built to expand human agency and opportunity, not to facilitate criminal activity. The events of the last week have shown the value of SHIELD to find suspicious activity before things escalate too far, as well as to accelerate resolution so the vast majority of legitimate users are not affected. Confidentiality cannot come at the expense of lawfulness and I strongly believe it doesn’t have to.

We’ve learned a great deal from this incident and work is already underway to harden our security systems and further adapt to the changing cybersecurity landscape. AI may be accelerating exploits, but it can also help us defend against them. I hope our entire industry responds with vigilance and feels the same sense of urgency to work together.

thank you g, appreciate you

a few random notes about this topic from my time running @collab_currency 

in general 

i remain a big believer that we should be using the internet and blockchains to open up better access to ideas, projects, and opportunities at the very earliest stages

stuff like fair launches, PoW, and cap formation tools

all of this extends from the same design principle of more equitable ownership formation

which i am very much inspired by and oriented toward

all that said

teams at the earliest stages still need a combo of tools in the toolkit for a higher probability of success

the three i usually point to are:

- capital
- connectivity
- counsel

capital gives founders room to hire, experiment, build

connectivity is the invisible and visible networks that help founders better find users, first hires, customers, collaborators

counsel is the experience from others around the project that can help founders work through hard decisions with people who’ve seen similar challenges before

so all this to say

at the very earliest stages, crypto/blockchains have started to become an amazing tool at pooling capital together for founders and projects

but i have found that it has had a harder time with the other two (connectivity, counsel)

which is the stuff after the capital arrives

i am talking my book a bit

but i'm also pretty optimistic that these two don't necessarily have to come from a pre-seed/seed stage investor in the future

over time i’d love to see those parts of the venture model unbundled

until then, i think i think there's a tremendous amount of value to be created 

showing up for founders at the earliest stages

helping them navigate their project to higher ground

standing behind them as they do the tough stuff

text:
.@CadeMarket turned 1 a few days ago.

I want to reflect back on the last year that i've been working on this and share some of the lore for the many new eyes we have on the project now.

A year ago I deployed the token on Pump Fun for what was then a very VERY different project. I took a ROM of 2048 and let users play collaboratively via typing commands in a Pump Fun livestream chat.

Shortly after, I made a dozen or so arcade games with the same sort of premise. You typed "play" in the chat and you'd join the minigame and it would simulate the game outcome. Over a week or so, I gave out creator fees from the token to players on the leaderboard. Every few days, I turned on the livestream and people would play. This went on for a few weeks.

At this point, I was still employed full time as a smart contract engineer, and Cade was just a fun side project i'd work on late at night.

I had a random thought pop into my head one night. What if I could let people bet on the outcome of the games, and I built a system to let users control a wallet via live stream commands.

This one idea made me so delusionally optimistic about building Cade that I made the (at the time) crazy decision to quit my job. Mind you, my wife and I had just had our first child, and he was 2 months old.

For the next 6 months, I was working full-time on the project... for free. Didn't want to touch the creator fees of the token.

During this time, the idea began to evolve. I dropped the livestream aspect to the project, and realized that the tech that I had built was quite literally picture perfect for resolving markets programmatically. Because I could resolve a market programmatically, this opened up the possibility to offer very short prediction markets.

This was where the modern day idea of Cade was born. Quick markets, on only things that can be verifiably resolved, paid out instantly.

In March, I was selected as a winner of the Pump Fun build in public hackathon. The hilarious part of this is that @kosgoood ran the hackathon, and later joined Cade as my Chief Operating Officer.

A day after winning the hackathon, I had already closed a pre-seed fundraising round. Less than 2 weeks later, I closed a seed fundraising round.

At this point, we were ready to hyperscale the tech. My first 2 hires were @gnarzilla as CTO and @steoniy as CPO, both of which i've known and worked with prior. 

Shortly after that, I brought on @0xRookmate and @scottybmitch, 2 more engineers that i've known for years.

Before the summer, we ran an open beta. This was to introduce users to the general premise of Cade. We intentionally put out a very raw version of the product. This resulted in users giving us VERY constructive feedback, and we listened to every single piece of it.

This has been a trend for Cade. We always build everything (that we can) in public, and it's been one of the best business decisions that i've made.

In July, it was time to introduce sports markets. We ran the Cade Cup, which was a short duration prediction market tournament on World Cup games. The traction for this was massive. Around 10,000 active users and nearly 200k predictions.

In mid September, we wanted to stress test the systems again. We launched Meme Madness, which would give us 22 hours of live platform activity. Once again, the traction was staggering. Roughly 14,000 users and over half a million predictions.

All throughout this time, we spent 3 months putting hours and hours a day into legal and research on what would be required to launch the platform in the most legally compliant manner.

At the end of August, we were able to obtain the necessary iGaming license that will permit our mainnet launch with real dollars on the platform.

That's all for now.

I'll see you all for the Cade mainnet launch.

Today we're unveiling Trillium Labs @trillium_labs, a new non-profit to foster the open science of frontier AI. We're building open post-training recipes and will expand into open infra to study RSI, reward-hacking, multi-agent systems, and whatever comes next.

We're built around the theory of change that you need more eyes to solve hard technical problems. We have faith in the scientific methods and communities that humanity has built, and worry that AI is becoming too closed to utilize them.

Trilliums are wildflowers that bloom briefly in the spring, before the forest canopies fill out. Though they are small, they lay the foundation for the cycles of growth and nourishment through the rest of the year. At Trillium Labs, the recipes will be the slow nutrients for the seasons and the model releases will be the blooms. Building an institution dedicated to this is needed because, much as nature’s trilliums are slow to expand and grow, the open-ecosystem needs time and dedicated resources to catch up.

I co-founded with with a long-time friend and collaborator Tom Zick (@thesezickbeats). We're hiring (full time + student collabs/interns), we're fundraising, and we're looking for compute. Please get in touch if you're interested in helping out. Offices based in the Bay Area and Cambridge MA, remote okay.

I’m in the Bay Area until for The Curve and COLM to connect with people who are interested. We’re thankful to have initial support from Halcyon Futures and Schmidt Sciences with more funding en route to enable our ambitions of scaling. text:
NEAR AI has claimed first place on the Lean Eval v1 leaderboard.

Lean Eval v1 is an active benchmark maintained by Lean FRO that contains extremely hard formalization problems. We reached first place despite joining the competition just four weeks ago, a full month later than other top participants.

NEAR is very heavily investing in formal verification efforts. Our ultimate goal is to formally prove the protocol and all the core contracts, and to provide a practical tool for others to formally verify their contracts in a fast and affordable way.

The system that enabled us to claim first place is almost entirely powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and thus is (a) extremely cheap, and (b) has no dependencies on third parties because the model is open weight.

When it comes to formally verifying software, the approach boils down to three pillars:
1. Representing the program in a way that can be reasoned about;
2. Expressing the properties that we desire to prove;
3. Coming up with a proof and formalizing it in Lean.

Until recently, step (3) was prohibitively expensive for practical use at scale. With the system that we used for Lean Eval, we now have it solved. Stay tuned for updates on how we apply it in practice to formally verify NEAR contracts.

text:
a16z's Seema Amble on why AI-native startups still beat incumbents: the incumbent owns the system of record, the startup owns the whole job.

"Why do you need an AI-native startup if you've got Claudeforce... You've got all your data, and your employees are used to the product. So why another product?"

"I absolutely still think there's a case for the AI-native startup, and it centers around the fact that the legacy incumbent is limited to their system of record, and they're not completing the end-to-end job."

"Say a customer calls and says they got charged after they cancelled. Resolving that isn't just the customer going into the chat and saying 'Hey, I got overcharged.'"

"The response there has to hit billing, it has to look at all the chat history, it has to look at the contract. That's not one system of record, that's the knowledge around that customer and everything it touched."

"The opportunity for the AI-native startup is to say: we're going to own that entire end-to-end arc. That could be legal, owning everything from brief all the way through trial... It's really the concept of owning the end-to-end work."

Lio co-founder and CEO Vladimir Keil joins a16z's Seema Amble and Elena Burger to discuss where AI-native startups have an advantage when incumbent software companies already own the customer, the data, and the system of record:

Their answer comes down to the work that happens outside those systems. In procurement, a final price in an ERP can hide hundreds of emails, spreadsheets, supplier conversations, engineering analyses, and decisions across legal, finance, and operations. Vlad explains how Lio uses multi-agent systems to take on more of that end-to-end work, from sourcing and RFQs to negotiation, shipment tracking, and invoices.

They also discuss how enterprises learn to trust agents with increasingly consequential decisions, why the last 20% of an internal AI build can require most of the effort, and what happens when both buyers and suppliers have agents working on their behalf.

quoted_text:
Blast will be shutting down.

We launched Blast with the goal of building a self-sustaining chain for users and developers. Unfortunately, the economics of operating the chain no longer make sense: the ongoing costs of maintaining Blast exceed the revenue generated by the L2, and we do not see a credible path to making the chain economically sustainable.

As a result, we've made the difficult decision to wind Blast down.

We're sorry to the users and developers who believed in Blast, built on it, and supported the ecosystem. Our priority now is making the shutdown as smooth and safe as possible.

We're asking all users to withdraw their assets from Blast to Ethereum mainnet, including any balances held in the Blast PWA.

To make this easier, we will be reducing the withdrawal delay to 24 hours.

As part of the shutdown process, we'll first begin withdrawing Blast's Lido assets. This process is expected to take approximately one week. During this period, withdrawals will temporarily be unavailable, even after the withdrawal delay is reduced to 24 hours.

Once that process is complete, withdrawals will resume with the new 24-hour delay.

Users will have until October 26, 2026 to withdraw through the normal Blast interface.

After October 26, assets will remain withdrawable, but users will need to interact directly with the Blast bridge contracts on Ethereum L1. We'll publish detailed instructions before then.

We strongly encourage everyone to withdraw their assets to Ethereum mainnet before October 26.

I’m watching three friends lose 11 lbs of body weight in a race car tomorrow

+ Tobias Lutke (founder shopify)
+ DHH (creator ruby on rails)
+ Mathias Beche (le mans podium)
 
Race car driving is insane… 

+ 122°F cockpit
+ heart rate 170
+ 2.5 hours straight
+ 10 hr race 
+ up to 4.2 g force (wild)
+ multi-layer fireproof suit
+ sweat barely evaporate
+ 600-900 calories per hour

The race is a 10-hour endurance track in atlanta.  It’s called Motul Petit Le Mans. 

Tomorrow is the season finale, where 54 cars across multiple classes run roughly 400 laps of the 2.54-mile road. The race doesn’t end till 10 pm.

They’ll be driving an LMP2: 
+ 603 horsepower
+ 2,050 pounds
+ 9,000 rpm

I’ve personally experienced some of the above things:

> core body temp of 102°F
> 3 g force in my airplane 
> non evaporative clothing 
> stomping 200 lbs
> severe dehydration

text:
I think a lot of people are feeling what @CryptoGideon_ is feeling right now, and I genuinely recommend taking a break for as long as you need.

These are signs of burnout, and it can spiral into depression, an endless loop that’s hard to climb out of.

Deep down, you’ll want to push for “just one more click,” but that’s exactly the trap.

When your judgment is already clouded, you start forcing trades, over-leveraging, or going all-in to “make it back.”

Most times, that ends with your entire portfolio getting wiped out in a single liquidation.

Log off. Step away from anything crypto-related. Exercise. Fix your sleep cycle and bad habits. Get more sunlight. Read a book. Pick some new skills.

Do anything that improves your mental and physical health.

Once you’re recharged, you can come back with a fresh perspective and a much much clearer mind or even found your real calling.

Honestly, no one’s going to blame you. It’s just you and your mind. Bear or bull, crypto or not, you only have one job: survive and make it the best life you can, literally and figuratively.

And hopefully for crypto fellas, you’ll make it or maybe even retire at the end of it all. No guarantee, but that's the beauty of life itself.

Just, be kind to yourself.

Following gold-medal-level performance from our AI models across five competitions in mathematics, physics, and chemistry, we asked a harder question: can AI contribute when a problem is genuinely open and without an existing solution path?

Over the past several months, mathematicians worked with Muse Spark 1.1 and Muse Spark 1.2 in Thinking Mode through the regular https://t.co/wHkMPH82ZH chat interface, with no custom research scaffold, to find solutions to such problems.

Our goal wasn't to mass-produce papers, but empower researchers. Every collaboration followed the same principles: mathematicians guided the research, a second group of mathematicians then reviewed the work, each paper marks which passages were drafted primarily by humans or AI, and each credits the prior research it builds on. Where other teams independently announced solutions to the same problems, we acknowledge their work as well.

Today, we're sharing six papers from that collaboration.

quoted_text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

NEAR AI has claimed first place on the Lean Eval v1 leaderboard.

Lean Eval v1 is an active benchmark maintained by Lean FRO that contains extremely hard formalization problems. We reached first place despite joining the competition just four weeks ago, a full month later than other top participants.

NEAR is very heavily investing in formal verification efforts. Our ultimate goal is to formally prove the protocol and all the core contracts, and to provide a practical tool for others to formally verify their contracts in a fast and affordable way.

The system that enabled us to claim first place is almost entirely powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and thus is (a) extremely cheap, and (b) has no dependencies on third parties because the model is open weight.

When it comes to formally verifying software, the approach boils down to three pillars:
1. Representing the program in a way that can be reasoned about;
2. Expressing the properties that we desire to prove;
3. Coming up with a proof and formalizing it in Lean.

Until recently, step (3) was prohibitively expensive for practical use at scale. With the system that we used for Lean Eval, we now have it solved. Stay tuned for updates on how we apply it in practice to formally verify NEAR contracts.

text:
DeFi might be solving the wrong liquidity problem.

we've spent years optimizing pools, routing, aggregators and solver competition under the assumption that liquidity is the scarce resource. but as execution becomes more asynchronous and intents become more expressive, i think the real bottleneck increasingly becomes balance sheet capacity.

consider an asynchronous cross-venue trade. a solver can find the liquidity and construct the optimal route, but between initiation and settlement someone still has to own the ugly intermediate states: partial fills, inventory exposure, venue failures, price movement and settlement latency. absorbing those risks requires capital.

TradFi has entire businesses built around this. dealers warehouse inventory, prime brokers finance positions, clearing members guarantee obligations and repo markets finance the balance sheets underneath it all. the visible trade is only one layer of the financial system.

crypto currently bundles a lot of this into solvers and market makers. we describe solver competition as an execution problem: better routing, better pricing, better search. but two solvers running equally good algorithms are not equivalent if one can warehouse $100m of risk while the other needs to remain inventory-neutral.

as intents become more expressive and execution becomes increasingly asynchronous, i think balance sheet capacity itself eventually becomes something we need to price and compose. an executor shouldn't necessarily have to warehouse every intermediate risk itself; another participant could underwrite that execution subject to explicit collateral, duration and exposure constraints, while another market finances the inventory underneath it.

that potentially separates two businesses we currently bundle together: finding the best execution and being willing to financially guarantee that execution.

routing algorithms will commoditize. credible capital willing to stand behind outcomes probably won't.

liquidity tells you whether a trade can happen. balance sheet capacity determines who can promise that it will.

text:
after years of running and advising GTMs, i can confidently say the biggest lesson i have learned is that "perfect is the enemy of great."

it is impossible to resonate with every single prospective audience member. it is impossible to please every single internal stakeholder

and if you optimize for the above, you have marketing that falls flat and fails to move the needle. there is no way around it

you can tell when something is corpo slop/when there were clearly 6+ stakeholders involved in the process. when too many people provided input on a launch video and there's no clear message or a message that isn't compelling

marketing is supposed to be controversial. it's supposed to be thought provoking. somewhere along the line i think many of us have forgotten that and it's become increasingly cookie cutter and playbook oriented. it's become a function that follows orders instead of setting trends or resonating with tastemakers

i encourage everyone to experiment more boldly and not to be so afraid of worst case scenarios. attention is fickle and you need to win it early and keep winning it

if we depend on product folks to keep shipping for retention, it's on us to solve the cold start problem and bring in eyeballs

PSA for new Revoke Ultimate subscribers 🛡️

After last week's Magic Eden exploit, we've seen quite a few new Ultimate subscribers.

Thank you for the trust! Please take 2 minutes to check your setup. Auto-Revoking can only protect a wallet when both of these are true:

1. You granted auto-revoke permissions for that wallet in MetaMask
2. Your wallet is a MetaMask smart account on that network

Step 2 usually happens automatically during step 1. But the upgrade can fail (e.g. if you've already upgraded to a smart account with another wallet).

How to check:
→ Go to https://t.co/awlDyR8hgv
→ Open the Auto-Revoking section
→ Look for a yellow warning banner or a ⚠️ icon next to a network. Each one marks a network where you are NOT protected yet.

How to fix it:
→ Switch the account to a smart account in MetaMask
→ If a different wallet app already upgraded your address, switch it back to a regular account in that app first. Then upgrade it in MetaMask.

Also check that every network you use is toggled on, and that each wallet in your subscription granted its own permissions.

If something is unclear, our DMs and Discord are open 🙏

author: a16z
quoted_text:
Lio co-founder and CEO Vladimir Keil joins a16z's Seema Amble and Elena Burger to discuss where AI-native startups have an advantage when incumbent software companies already own the customer, the data, and the system of record:

Their answer comes down to the work that happens outside those systems. In procurement, a final price in an ERP can hide hundreds of emails, spreadsheets, supplier conversations, engineering analyses, and decisions across legal, finance, and operations. Vlad explains how Lio uses multi-agent systems to take on more of that end-to-end work, from sourcing and RFQs to negotiation, shipment tracking, and invoices.

They also discuss how enterprises learn to trust agents with increasingly consequential decisions, why the last 20% of an internal AI build can require most of the effort, and what happens when both buyers and suppliers have agents working on their behalf.

IoTeX v2.5.0 (Zanzibar Hardfork) is officially out! 🌐

MainNet activation: Block 53,533,081 (est. Oct 19, 02:00 UTC).

This is a massive protocol upgrade that moves staking rewards fully on-chain, tightens EVM precision, and lays the security groundwork for our next phase of scalability.

Here is how it impacts the network:

🗳️ 1. Fully Decentralized Staking Rewards (IIP-59)
- The Tech: Voter rewards are now natively computed and distributed by the protocol itself at era boundaries (24 epochs).
- The Impact: Zero reliance on off-chain services (like Hermes). Staking yields are now 100% trustless and automated. We’ve designed this for a seamless transition—most Hermes-vault delegates with complete reward portions will be migrated automatically at the fork block.

⚡️ 2. EVM Precision & Gas Savings
- The Tech: Corrected GetCommittedState for absent prestates and fixed SELFDESTRUCT transfer-log amounts.
- The Impact: Strict compliance with EIP-2200 dynamic gas rules. For developers and users, this prevents massive gas overcharging on certain in-place writes (saving 2,800 gas per hit). For indexers and wallets, token balance histories reconstructed from tx logs are now perfectly accurate.

🛡️ 3. Proactive Security (BLS PoP)
- The Tech: BLS proof-of-possession is now enforced on candidate register/update operations.
- The Impact: This completely closes the rogue-key forgery window today, safely paving the runway for IIP-52 signature aggregation (massive network scalability) tomorrow. (Note: Providing a BLS key is now optional until IIP-52 is live).

🖥️ 4. Zero-Friction Upgrades for Node Operators
- The Tech: The hardfork heights and new contract addresses are baked directly into the binary.
- The Impact: No genesis replacements. No config changes. Just a pure, clean binary roll. 👉 docker pull iotex/iotex-core:v2.5.0 and restart.

text:
Work-life balance is a lie people tell themselves to justify mediocrity. What actually exists, for the people I respect most, is the ability to toggle between work mode and personal mode seamlessly, sometimes even simultaneously. 

It isn't multitasking in the bad sense. It's no longer treating work and life as two separate rooms you have to walk between all day. The people who pull this off share a few things:

1. They genuinely love what they do, so a call at an odd hour doesn't trigger anxiety, it triggers curiosity. They have real ownership and equity in what  they're building, so the extra hours feel like investment instead of extraction. 

2. They've developed enough emotional maturity to know the difference between urgency and habit. And they've all quietly abandoned the 9 to 5 as a container, trading it for something looser, work folded into life all day long instead of rationed into a block. 

The lesson isn't that everyone should be reachable all the time. It's that being reachable only works once you've stopped treating work and personal time as competing for the same hour. 

Most people burn out trying to protect a wall between the two. The ones who thrive stopped building the wall in the first place.

text: As a successful gambling addict I just cannot relate to people who go into the red and lose it all and have no discipline or self control
author: DeeZe
quoted_text:
Meet Thomas, a 35-year-old who got hooked to FanDuel and DraftKings in the pandemic, ended up $50,000 in the red. He filed for bankruptcy and signed up for a Pennsylvania registry that banned him from using betting apps.

More recently, he saw an ad for Kalshi offering a cash bonus. He got the app and couldn’t put it down. He’s now living with his mom and grandmother and taking loans from them to afford food and car insurance payments. “I have a gambling addiction” he wrote to Kalshi, begging for them to ban him, which they eventually did. But not before he was more than $25,000 in the hole. 

Thomas represents dark side of the prediction market boom: Problem gamblers who relapse with Kalshi, which has blanketed TV, social media, sports stadiums, bus stations, trains, with ads trying to attract new traders, just as they insist they are not a gambling operator. That means they don’t honor “self-exclusion” registries maintained by states like Pennsylvania. Mental health clinicians say that creates a loophole for people like Thomas. 

What really got Thomas were Kalshi’s 15-minute crypto markets, where you can make a binary trade on whether Bitcoin will be above or below a certain number every 15 minutes. There were times he was betting 18 hours a day in these markets. 

He told me: “The odds flip so quickly. It’s such a rush. And when I’d lose, my brain just kept wanting to win it back. I never even traded Bitcoin or any crypto, but I just kept coming back to the rush of how unpredictable the markets were.”

A clinician I spoke to called 15-minute crypto markets “a slot machine in your pocket”

Following NEAR AI topping putnambench leaderboard, we now have claimed #1 on Lean Eval v1, the official active benchmark maintained by the Lean developers. 

We now have a very capable and cheap formal verification agent, and will share how we use it to formally prove NEAR protocol and smart contracts soon.
author: AlexSkidanov
quoted_text:
NEAR AI has claimed first place on the Lean Eval v1 leaderboard.

Lean Eval v1 is an active benchmark maintained by Lean FRO that contains extremely hard formalization problems. We reached first place despite joining the competition just four weeks ago, a full month later than other top participants.

NEAR is very heavily investing in formal verification efforts. Our ultimate goal is to formally prove the protocol and all the core contracts, and to provide a practical tool for others to formally verify their contracts in a fast and affordable way.

The system that enabled us to claim first place is almost entirely powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and thus is (a) extremely cheap, and (b) has no dependencies on third parties because the model is open weight.

When it comes to formally verifying software, the approach boils down to three pillars:
1. Representing the program in a way that can be reasoned about;
2. Expressing the properties that we desire to prove;
3. Coming up with a proof and formalizing it in Lean.

Until recently, step (3) was prohibitively expensive for practical use at scale. With the system that we used for Lean Eval, we now have it solved. Stay tuned for updates on how we apply it in practice to formally verify NEAR contracts.

Chainalysis Attributes Bitget’s $387M Hack to DPRK Actors, Traces Funds Across Four Chains

Chainalysis said the $387 million Bitget hack was carried out by DPRK-linked threat actors. Within the first three hours, the stolen funds moved across Ethereum, XRP, Zcash and Tron through 23 transfers, with Ethereum and XRP accounting for 49.7% and 40.8% respectively. Investigators also traced tens of millions of dollars in stolen XRP through cross-chain liquidity protocols into Bitcoin over roughly a day and a half. The attack has pushed total DPRK-linked crypto thefts in 2026 above $1 billion.

text: Fun story of how we met @fredwilson and @uninsightful  and how USV investment in fomo came together.
author: paulerlanger
quoted_text:
Writing a check doesn’t qualify you to give advice.

When @fredwilson was 29 he tried to show up to a board meeting and start giving advice. One of the founders stopped him, “come do every job in the company for a week, then we’ll listen.” So he flew to Buffalo and did it.

With @uninsightful staying at USV as an Investment Partner, I asked the two of them to sit down and compare notes on a business they entered almost four decades apart.

Nikhil is the first analyst in our program’s 20-year history that we've offered the opportunity to stay and move up in the firm.

They covered earning a founder’s trust, building conviction before your partners agree, and staying open to ideas that challenge your strongest held beliefs. They also got into where USV has been right, where we’ve been (very) wrong, and how the venture business is changing.

Let's be honest about crypto for a second. For most of the last decade, it earned every bit of its bad reputation from tokens with no product, fortunes won and lost on speculation, and nothing real ever getting built.

The whole world looked at it and saw a casino, and they were mostly right.

That is exactly why Bittensor ($TAO) matters.

While the rest of crypto was spinning the wheel, Bittensor became something else. A place where a token is tied to actual work. Across the network, subnets are producing real intelligence, training real models, doing genuine research, output that exists whether the token pumps or not.

The reward is not for hype. The reward is for building something that works.

That is the shift almost nobody outside is paying attention to yet. One corner of crypto is still launching coins about frogs. This corner is quietly building infrastructure the real world can use.

And that is what redemption looks like for an industry. Not a better casino. A reason to exist.

Somewhere in that network, we are building our piece of it. The control layer that keeps AI from going rogue. Because control over AI cannot belong to one company holding the keys behind closed doors. It has to live on a network no one owns, and Bittensor is the only thing ever built to meet that bar.

So the next time someone says crypto is all gambling, point them here. Not to a casino. To the place crypto finally grew up.

This is not another token to flip. It is a network building things that matter, and we are proud to be one of them.

text:
How do you feel about AI?

A common sentiment is that of a loss. This must be especially common among adults.

If you are 50 and you have been programming in Python for the last 25 years... it is a shock to find out that an AI agent can code faster than you can.

In a sense, it is like having lived on a continent all your life, where you hunted with bows and arrows... and then strange men come in with guns.

There is a divergence in society.

Some of us have been frustrated by the lack of progress. We don't like what has been happening to our civilization since 1970. We expected lunar bases, rejuvenation cures, cancer cures, space trips... and all we got was Twitter.

When the Spanish arrived in America, they immediately found many allies.

Cortés landed on the Gulf coast with roughly 500 men, mostly young men (Cortés was 34). They had a handful of horses, crossbows and arquebuses. He had no army to speak of.

Yet this small band laid siege to Mexico, helped by 50x or 100x indigenous warriors from various tribes. This all happened within 2 years.

It is hard to know exactly what happened, but it seems quite clear that many people were frustrated with the current state of affairs.

I feel the same regarding AI. Finally, there is an opening.

Don't get me wrong. I don't mindlessly jump on new technologies. I buy paper books, a paper newspaper and I carry paper notebooks. I only got a smartphone in 2018. I still code every day in C++ even though I am constantly told that it is obsolete.

But what I care about is progress taken broadly. And I feel that this has been stolen from me.

Far from getting cancer cures, the medical system in Quebec is still based on faxes.

I feel that the people who love stagnation got enough of what they wanted and I hope that we are at an inflexion point where we finally break free from the oppressive rule of stagnation.

Contrary to what you will hear, stagnation does not keep you safe. It puts you at risk. Both individually and collectively. Individually, the lack of progress means that you will die earlier than you could have. Collectively... stagnation makes you vulnerable as the Aztec found out.

There is a political angle to the story.

In Quebec, a major politician was recently 'caught'. He launched a book just prior to the campaign. And it was revealed that the book had been written by AI. Far from apologizing, the politician came clean and even said that we should use AI more.

Much of the political sphere in the West is occupied by people who hold power based on a zero-sum strategy. There is no growth and there is possibly even a decline. It is all a matter of deciding how we share the fixed pie.

There is another way, one where everyone gets more, much more. But it requires a different type of politics... one that is less adversarial and more permissive... with the downside that you have less control about who gets what.

I think, I hope, that we are at a crossroads where the West will seek abundance, and we will renew with the pre-1970 approach that served us so well.

Of course, they are monsters lurking. But I am up for the adventure.

text:
最近看了《一人企业》（Paul Jarvis），里面有一个核心思想让我很有共鸣：

企业不一定要变大，变得更好、更自由、更可控，同样是一种成功。

顺着这个逻辑，我突然想到：

如果把“一人企业”的哲学，放到交易上，会变成什么？

⸻

01｜增长

一人企业：

增长不一定是目标。

变好，而不是变大，才是一人企业的核心。

一人交易员：

收益增长也不应该是唯一目标。

提高判断力、执行力、风控能力和资金效率，比单纯追求账户规模更重要。

账户变大，不等于交易能力变强。

⸻

02｜规模

一人企业：

小规模不是创业的过渡阶段。

小规模本身就可以是终点。

一人交易员：

不是所有交易员都必须管理几千万、几个亿。

如果一个人用自己的系统获得了足够的收益，同时拥有时间自由，

小资金也可以是一种完整的成功。

规模是选项，不是义务。

⸻

03｜控制权

一人企业：

可以外包，可以合作，但必须牢牢掌握决策权和控制权。

一人交易员：

可以使用AI、量化工具、数据、策略、程序和外部研究，

但最终必须知道：

为什么下注、下注多少、什么时候退出。

工具可以替你执行，

但不能替你承担风险。

⸻

04｜自由职业

一人企业：

自由职业是出售时间换取收入。

一人企业则是搭建系统，把能力变成资产。

一人交易员：

每天盯盘、不断交易，并不代表交易能力越来越强。

真正的进化是：

经验 → 规则 → 策略 → 系统。

让过去的经验不断沉淀成可以重复使用的交易资产。

⸻

05｜客户选择

一人企业：

不必讨好所有客户。

宁愿服务少量优质客户，也不要承接大量消耗自己的客户。

一人交易员：

也不必交易所有行情。

市场每天都有机会，

但不是每一个机会都属于你。

只交易自己真正理解、验证过、有优势的行情。

⸻

06｜拒绝

一人企业：

不是所有订单都值得接。

糟糕的客户，赚再多钱也可能不值得。

一人交易员：

不是所有交易都值得做。

没有赔率的交易、看不懂的交易、情绪驱动的交易、为了FOMO而做的交易，

即使偶尔赚钱，也不代表它是好交易。

赚钱不等于做对。

⸻

07｜客户复购

一人企业：

老客户的复购和转介绍，通常比不断寻找新客户更高效。

一人交易员：

已经验证过的交易优势，比不断寻找新指标、新策略更加重要。

不要今天MACD，

明天RSI，

后天均线，

看到一个新指标就重新建立信仰。

真正的优势，是能够重复。

⸻
author: hazenlee

text:
08｜产品

一人企业：

尽量把一次性的经验，变成可以反复售卖的数字产品。

从出售时间，转向出售资产。

一人交易员：

也应该把一次性的交易经验，变成可以重复执行的交易系统。

一笔盈利只是结果。

如果能把：

为什么赚？

为什么亏？

什么环境有效？

什么环境失效？

什么时候加仓？

什么时候减仓？

全部沉淀下来，

一次交易才能真正变成自己的资产。

⸻

09｜MVP

一人企业：

不要等产品完美才上线。

先做最小可用版本，然后不断迭代。

一人交易员：

不要等策略完美才开始。

可以用小仓位验证：

假设 → 实盘 → 数据 → 复盘 → 修正。

交易系统不是想出来的，

而是在真实市场里迭代出来的。

⸻

10｜自动化

一人企业：

能自动化的工作，就不要人工硬扛。

短期任务可以外包，不轻易扩大固定成本。

一人交易员：

能程序化监控的，不要靠自己24小时盯盘。

能条件单执行的，不要完全依赖临场情绪。

能用数据验证的，不要靠主观争论。

高级交易不是让自己越来越忙，而是让系统越来越强。

⸻

11｜机会

一人企业：

机会很多，但人的时间有限。

警惕FOMO，学会筛选机会。

一人交易员：

市场里的机会更多。

BTC、ETH、美股、黄金、外汇、商品……

每天都有上涨和下跌。

但真正重要的问题不是：

“哪里有机会？”

而是：

“什么机会属于我的系统？”

⸻

12｜欲望

一人企业：

收入提高以后，不要同步拉高生活开销。

开销越大，自由越少。

一人交易员：

收益提高以后，也不要同步提高收益目标。

如果赚10万以后，必须赚20万才能满足；

赚100万以后，又必须赚200万；

那么账户增长再快，

自由依然不会到来。

⸻

13｜现金流

一人企业：

从创业第一天就赚钱，同时预留现金储备，应对淡季。

一人交易员：

永远给自己留现金。

不要让全部资本都暴露在市场里。

因为：

现金不是没有收益的资产，而是等待机会的期权。

没有现金，

就没有选择权。

⸻

14｜资本

一人企业：

资本可以带来增长，但融资也会带来约束。

钱越多，责任和外部压力可能越大。

一人交易员：

管理别人的钱，也意味着承担别人的预期。

收益目标、回撤限制、赎回压力、业绩考核……

资本规模增加的同时，

交易自由也可能减少。

资本越多，不一定越自由。

⸻

15｜成功

一人企业：

很多企业做大以后，创始人却失去了生活。

赢了规模，输了自由。

这不一定是成功。

一人交易员：

很多交易员也是如此。

账户越来越大，

仓位越来越重，

盯盘越来越久，

精神压力越来越大，

最后：

赚到了钱，却失去了生活。

这同样值得重新思考。

⸻

最后

《一人企业》真正让我思考的，不是“一人”这两个字。

而是：

你到底是在建立一个服务自己人生的系统，还是把自己变成系统的奴隶？

一人企业如此。

一人交易员同样如此。

交易的终点，不一定是：

更大的本金、更高的收益、更大的仓位。

也可以是：

更强的认知、更稳定的系统、更低的时间占用，以及更大的选择权。

所以：

变大，是选项，不是义务。

盈利，是结果，不是人生目的。

足够，远比更多重要。

控制权，比规模更珍贵。

交易应该服务于自由，而不是让自由成为交易的抵押品。

quoted_text:
I’m watching three friends lose 11 lbs of body weight in a race car tomorrow

+ Tobias Lutke (founder shopify)
+ DHH (creator ruby on rails)
+ Mathias Beche (le mans podium)
 
Race car driving is insane… 

+ 122°F cockpit
+ heart rate 170
+ 2.5 hours straight
+ 10 hr race 
+ up to 4.2 g force (wild)
+ multi-layer fireproof suit
+ sweat barely evaporate
+ 600-900 calories per hour

The race is a 10-hour endurance track in atlanta.  It’s called Motul Petit Le Mans. 

Tomorrow is the season finale, where 54 cars across multiple classes run roughly 400 laps of the 2.54-mile road. The race doesn’t end till 10 pm.

They’ll be driving an LMP2: 
+ 603 horsepower
+ 2,050 pounds
+ 9,000 rpm

I’ve personally experienced some of the above things:

> core body temp of 102°F
> 3 g force in my airplane 
> non evaporative clothing 
> stomping 200 lbs
> severe dehydration

But never all at once… inside a race car for 2.5 hours straight, competing for tenths of a second, and in a high risk environment. 

I’m struggling to get my head around it.

Last week, Tobi and I were at a conference catching up. He and I have been friends for 15 years. 

Tobi and DHH were my first customers at my payments startup Braintree.  I’ll forever be grateful to them and DHH’s co-founder @jasonfried for giving my company life.

Tobi approaches racing as I do my body. Data, method and analysis. A closed loop game of continuous improvement.

Off the track, Tobi: 
+ founder and ceo of Shopify
+ 6 million+ merchants
+ $195 billion market cap
+ 20 yrs building

Off the track, DHH:
+ created Ruby on Rails
+ co-founder 37signals 
+ 20 yrs building
+ profitable, no outside capital
+ 24 Hours of Le Mans class winner

On the track, Mathias Beche:
+ 24 Hours of Le Mans podium finisher
+ European Le Mans Series LMP2
+ FIA Endurance Championship winner
+ 15+ career prototype victories

What a team of bad asses. 

I’m excited to be in the pit on tomorrow and watch all of this go down.

quoted_text:
Blast will be shutting down.

We launched Blast with the goal of building a self-sustaining chain for users and developers. Unfortunately, the economics of operating the chain no longer make sense: the ongoing costs of maintaining Blast exceed the revenue generated by the L2, and we do not see a credible path to making the chain economically sustainable.

As a result, we've made the difficult decision to wind Blast down.

We're sorry to the users and developers who believed in Blast, built on it, and supported the ecosystem. Our priority now is making the shutdown as smooth and safe as possible.

We're asking all users to withdraw their assets from Blast to Ethereum mainnet, including any balances held in the Blast PWA.

To make this easier, we will be reducing the withdrawal delay to 24 hours.

As part of the shutdown process, we'll first begin withdrawing Blast's Lido assets. This process is expected to take approximately one week. During this period, withdrawals will temporarily be unavailable, even after the withdrawal delay is reduced to 24 hours.

Once that process is complete, withdrawals will resume with the new 24-hour delay.

Users will have until October 26, 2026 to withdraw through the normal Blast interface.

After October 26, assets will remain withdrawable, but users will need to interact directly with the Blast bridge contracts on Ethereum L1. We'll publish detailed instructions before then.

We strongly encourage everyone to withdraw their assets to Ethereum mainnet before October 26.

the line: under hidden-state transfer the survey lists as a limitation that the receiver "must share a similar backbone" with the sender

@mostik_ai first public result is a 753B model from one family handing state to a 4B from another, so I'd soften that to "the further the backbones, the more the bridge has to learn"
the survey was written before the summer's cross-family results (XBridge, Dual-Cache, ours) and I'd expect v4 to update it

text:
I’m watching three friends lose 11 lbs of body weight in a race car tomorrow

+ Tobias Lutke (founder shopify)
+ DHH (creator ruby on rails)
+ Mathias Beche (le mans podium)
 
Race car driving is insane… 

+ 122°F cockpit
+ heart rate 170
+ 2.5 hours straight
+ 10 hr race 
+ up to 4.2 g force (wild)
+ multi-layer fireproof suit
+ sweat barely evaporate
+ 600-900 calories per hour

The race is a 10-hour endurance track in atlanta.  It’s called Motul Petit Le Mans. 

Tomorrow is the season finale, where 54 cars across multiple classes run roughly 400 laps of the 2.54-mile road. The race doesn’t end till 10 pm.

They’ll be driving an LMP2: 
+ 603 horsepower
+ 2,050 pounds
+ 9,000 rpm

I’ve personally experienced some of the above things:

> core body temp of 102°F
> 3 g force in my airplane 
> non evaporative clothing 
> stomping 200 lbs
> severe dehydration

But never all at once… inside a race car for 2.5 hours straight, competing for tenths of a second, and in a high risk environment. 

I’m struggling to get my head around it.

Last week, Tobi and I were at a conference catching up. He and I have been friends for 15 years. 

Tobi and DHH were my first customers at my payments startup Braintree.  I’ll forever be grateful to them and DHH’s co-founder @jasonfried for giving my company life.

Tobi approaches racing as I do my body. Data, method and analysis. A closed loop game of continuous improvement.

Off the track, Tobi: 
+ founder and ceo of Shopify
+ 6 million+ merchants
+ $195 billion market cap
+ 20 yrs building

Off the track, DHH:
+ created Ruby on Rails
+ co-founder 37signals 
+ 20 yrs building
+ profitable, no outside capital
+ 24 Hours of Le Mans class winner

On the track, Mathias Beche:
+ 24 Hours of Le Mans podium finisher
+ European Le Mans Series LMP2
+ FIA Endurance Championship winner
+ 15+ career prototype victories

What a team of bad asses. 

I’m excited to be in the pit on tomorrow and watch all of this go down.

text:
OPENAI DOTS = A 24/7 AI COMPANY IN A BOX

@monokern wrote a great article on how to make the most of it.

Here are 10 steps summary 

Step 1 → Don't build chatbots.

Build persistent workers with their own cloud computer, browser, terminal, files, memory and schedules. They keep working after you close the laptop.

Step 2 → Give every agent one job.

A clear responsibility, clear sources, clear working rules and a clear point where human approval is required.

Step 3 → Appoint a Chief of Staff.

One Dot receives your objective, breaks it into tasks, delegates to specialists, checks the work and assembles the final output.

Step 4 → Remove yourself from agent handoffs.

Workers should receive only the context and tools they need, execute independently and report back to the orchestrator.

Step 5 → Give them real tools.

Connect Slack, Teams, Google Workspace, dashboards, APIs and authenticated browser sessions. Without tools, they're still just conversational agents.

Step 6 → Make workflows persistent.

Use schedules and triggers so monitoring, research, reporting and operational checks happen without anyone manually starting them.

Step 7 → Keep humans around the irreversible stuff.

Agents can read, research, analyze and draft. Sending, publishing, spending or changing important records should require approval.

Step 8 → Don't waste frontier models on everything.

Use the smartest model for orchestration and difficult judgment calls, then cheaper models for high-volume background work.

Step 9 → Give the whole team shared memory.

Keep project specs, decisions, pricing, approved claims and requirements in one persistent workspace.

Step 10 → Close the business loop.

Signal → research → outreach → execution → measurement → next action.

That’s where Dots gets really interesting.

You're no longer prompting AI one task at a time, you're designing a system that keeps operating after you log off.

Writing a check doesn’t qualify you to give advice.

With @uninsightful staying at USV as an Investment Partner, I asked the two of them to sit down and compare notes on a business they entered almost four decades apart.

Nikhil is the first analyst in our program’s 20-year history that we've offered the opportunity to stay and move up in the firm.

They covered earning a founder’s trust, building conviction before your partners agree, and staying open to ideas that challenge your strongest held beliefs. They also got into where USV has been right, where we’ve been (very) wrong, and how the venture business is changing.

text:
after years of running and advising GTMs, i can confidently say the biggest lesson i have learned is that "perfect is the enemy of great."

it is impossible to resonate with every single prospective audience member. it is impossible to please every single internal stakeholder

and if you optimize for the above, you have marketing that falls flat and fails to move the needle. there is no way around it

you can tell when something is corpo slop/when there were clearly 6+ stakeholders involved in the process. when too many people provided input on a launch video and there's no clear message or a message that isn't compelling

marketing is supposed to be controversial. it's supposed to be thought provoking. somewhere along the line i think many of us have forgotten that and it's become increasingly cookie cutter and playbook oriented. it's become a function that follows orders instead of setting trends or resonating with tastemakers

i encourage everyone to experiment more boldly and not to be so afraid of worst case scenarios. attention is fickle and you need to win it early and keep winning it

if we depend on product folks to keep shipping for retention, it's on us to solve the cold start problem and bring in eyeballs

author: ivanbogatyy
quoted_text:
NEAR AI has claimed first place on the Lean Eval v1 leaderboard.

Lean Eval v1 is an active benchmark maintained by Lean FRO that contains extremely hard formalization problems. We reached first place despite joining the competition just four weeks ago, a full month later than other top participants.

NEAR is very heavily investing in formal verification efforts. Our ultimate goal is to formally prove the protocol and all the core contracts, and to provide a practical tool for others to formally verify their contracts in a fast and affordable way.

The system that enabled us to claim first place is almost entirely powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and thus is (a) extremely cheap, and (b) has no dependencies on third parties because the model is open weight.

When it comes to formally verifying software, the approach boils down to three pillars:
1. Representing the program in a way that can be reasoned about;
2. Expressing the properties that we desire to prove;
3. Coming up with a proof and formalizing it in Lean.

Until recently, step (3) was prohibitively expensive for practical use at scale. With the system that we used for Lean Eval, we now have it solved. Stay tuned for updates on how we apply it in practice to formally verify NEAR contracts.

Phenomenal questions, so let's unpack them together.

First the serious answer, then a more pragmatic take from Everett Hildenbrandt, our CEO, to summarize it in 2 words.
 
1. Exhaustively, almost never (but that's fine).

Simply speaking, you leverage what comes from proving the handful of invariants that would be catastrophic if they broke. Then, you can compose those guarantees, module by module, instead of specifying the whole system at once.  
 
2. As far as better properties, if we start from asking 'what must never happen?' rather than 'what should happen?' then we're on the right path!
 
Fuzzing (or property-based tests) are also a cheap way to sharpen them before you commit to a proof.

With AI now handling more of the proof work in tools like Lean, Dafny and Verus, the bottleneck has shifted to the spec itself, but that raises a perhaps more interesting question: when code and proofs both get cheap to generate, does writing the spec become the new "coding", aka stating precisely what correct means?

But if you ask Everett, you'll get a half-jokingly "get good", as the simplest answer on how to write better properties in 2026 😅

很多人以为交易最大的难题是找到 Alpha。

其实不是。

你可以抓到 10x、100x，甚至连续抓对很多次，最后仍然把钱全部还给市场。

Discovery 和 Capital Retention 是两套完全不同的能力。

一个交易系统如果只负责「找到机会 → 买入」，却不负责「回收本金 → 隔离利润 → 限制重新下注」，那更强的 Alpha 发现能力，有时只是让你更快地扩大下一次下注。

最近我越来越觉得：

真正该优化的不是「我还能找到多少机会」，

而是

「每次找到机会以后，有多少利润最终永远离开风险池。」
author: runes_leo
quoted_text:
i quit. for good.💔

all i see on ct are people claiming to make 6–7 figures every month, but nobody really talks about people like me.

i’m 19 and made my first $30k in this space around the time trump launched his token. since then, i’ve managed to rinse through that entire $30k 

for the past two years, i’ve consistently lost around 5–10 sol every month, money that was supposed to be my allowance for going out and enjoying life. there have even been days when i’ve gone without food because i spent everything gambling on memecoins.

every time i load up, i get a little glimpse of what success could look like. whether it’s fumbling a potential $100k, calling 100x plays or making 10+ sol in a single day, i always find a way to give it all back.

when i’m down, i revenge trade trying to recover my losses. when i’m up, i get carried away, gamble more and oversize positions on absolute slop.

the worst part is that i’ve known these were my problems for over 10 months, yet i’ve done nothing to change my behaviour.

that’s why quitting feels like the smartest decision i can make right now.

i’ve completely lost my sense of the value of money because of this space. i’ve spent the past two years convincing myself that if i just keep going, stay hungry and never give up, eventually i’ll make it.

but sometimes, you need to accept that something isn’t working for you and have the courage to walk away.

the whole narrative about never quitting, staying hungry and grinding until you make it is often pushed by people selling courses and making their money off other people’s dreams.

in the past three days alone, i’ve lost roughly four times the average monthly salary in Canada, yet somehow, i still struggle to tell myself that enough is enough.

i’m not sharing this because i want donations or sympathy. i just wanted to share the perspective of someone who’s spent the past two years trying to make it in this space and ended up losing more than he gained.

not everyone on ct is making money. behind all the screenshots, winning trades and six figure claims, there are people quietly losing everything while trying to find their breakthrough.

sometimes, knowing when to walk away is also a form of winning.

i genuinely hope everyone reading this makes it. ❤️

author: LefterisJP
quoted_text:
Blast will be shutting down.

We launched Blast with the goal of building a self-sustaining chain for users and developers. Unfortunately, the economics of operating the chain no longer make sense: the ongoing costs of maintaining Blast exceed the revenue generated by the L2, and we do not see a credible path to making the chain economically sustainable.

As a result, we've made the difficult decision to wind Blast down.

We're sorry to the users and developers who believed in Blast, built on it, and supported the ecosystem. Our priority now is making the shutdown as smooth and safe as possible.

We're asking all users to withdraw their assets from Blast to Ethereum mainnet, including any balances held in the Blast PWA.

To make this easier, we will be reducing the withdrawal delay to 24 hours.

As part of the shutdown process, we'll first begin withdrawing Blast's Lido assets. This process is expected to take approximately one week. During this period, withdrawals will temporarily be unavailable, even after the withdrawal delay is reduced to 24 hours.

Once that process is complete, withdrawals will resume with the new 24-hour delay.

Users will have until October 26, 2026 to withdraw through the normal Blast interface.

After October 26, assets will remain withdrawable, but users will need to interact directly with the Blast bridge contracts on Ethereum L1. We'll publish detailed instructions before then.

We strongly encourage everyone to withdraw their assets to Ethereum mainnet before October 26.

Writing a check doesn’t qualify you to give advice.

When @fredwilson was 29 he tried to show up to a board meeting and start giving advice. One of the founders stopped him, “come do every job in the company for a week, then we’ll listen.” So he flew to Buffalo and did it.

With @uninsightful staying at USV as an Investment Partner, I asked the two of them to sit down and compare notes on a business they entered almost four decades apart.

Nikhil is the first analyst in our program’s 20-year history that we've offered the opportunity to stay and move up in the firm.

Surprised this hasn’t gotten more attention: Ethereum L1 is barely showing up in the tokenized equities boom.

Tokenized equities already account for 12% of spot DEX vol on-chain, yet Ethereum L1 has close to 0 market share.

Robinhood, Arbitrum and Base are doing the gruntwork obviously. But where does that leave the L1?

Tokenization is going to reshape  the onchain economy, and tokenized equities are going to be the  fastest-growing segment over the next 2 years. 

Ethereum needs a clear vision for what belongs on L1, what moves to L2s, and how the two fit together, from security and governance to liquidity and value accrual.

More on this in my article next week.

Following NEAR AI topping putnambench leaderboard, we now have claimed #1 on Lean Eval v1, the official active benchmark maintained by the Lean developers.

author: evan_van_ness
quoted_text:
NEAR AI has claimed first place on the Lean Eval v1 leaderboard.

Lean Eval v1 is an active benchmark maintained by Lean FRO that contains extremely hard formalization problems. We reached first place despite joining the competition just four weeks ago, a full month later than other top participants.

NEAR is very heavily investing in formal verification efforts. Our ultimate goal is to formally prove the protocol and all the core contracts, and to provide a practical tool for others to formally verify their contracts in a fast and affordable way.

The system that enabled us to claim first place is almost entirely powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and thus is (a) extremely cheap, and (b) has no dependencies on third parties because the model is open weight.

When it comes to formally verifying software, the approach boils down to three pillars:
1. Representing the program in a way that can be reasoned about;
2. Expressing the properties that we desire to prove;
3. Coming up with a proof and formalizing it in Lean.

Until recently, step (3) was prohibitively expensive for practical use at scale. With the system that we used for Lean Eval, we now have it solved. Stay tuned for updates on how we apply it in practice to formally verify NEAR contracts.

text:
SHIELD, in English.

@near_intents NEAR Intents has a risk screen. 

On a 1Click swap, before Intents fills your order, SHIELD checks it against known incidents and risk signals.

Think KYT, not KYC. It looks at the money, not your passport.

The signals come from both machines and people.

The docs describe a rule-based anomaly engine. Incidents can also be raised by partners, on-call operators and internal tooling. @AlexAuroraDev  says SHIELD also takes signals from analytics providers, researchers and large institutions.

If a flow is flagged:

before execution: no quote.
during execution: abort the swap and hold the funds.

That's what happened with the @bitget hacker.

$50M+ in attempted swaps flagged; most never got a quote.

~$503K stopped mid-swap.
~$166K got through.
Alex's figures, ±10%.

What SHIELD isn't: @NEARProtocol  consensus.

It doesn't freeze your wallet or stop the chain.
It's policy inside the Intents app deciding whether Intents will process the trade.

What isn't documented yet: where the rules end and human discretion begins, who can release a held swap, and what happens if SHIELD is wrong.

The chain can stay permissionless, and the order desk can still say no.

NEAR is the rail. Intents is the order desk. SHIELD is the screen at the desk.

Alex Shevchenko's Bitget report: https://t.co/5KKoYCtwz5
Illia on permissionless vs policy: https://t.co/khhXeBqcWY
SHIELD docs (Proactive Intents Security): https://t.co/ngsf0of4jh
SHIELD Incident API: https://t.co/n8Bp2YXSEL
author: Airdrops_one
quoted_text:
NEAR is permissionless programmable money.

Permissionless means nobody needs permission to own and transfer assets, or deploy contracts on NEAR.

It does not mean every application or liquidity provider must process every transaction.

SHIELD is how NEAR Intents applies this in practice: shared, real-time risk intelligence that lets participants identify hacks and other incidents and choose not to facilitate stolen funds. Partners can both consume and contribute incident data.

In the Bitget hack, SHIELD identified $50M+ in attempted flows through NEAR Intents and helped stop funds during execution.

Open financial infrastructure does not require us to make theft easy. Instead of hiding behind "it's permissionless, what can we do" while sitting on pause button, we should be creative in solutions that are addressing underlying problem.

We can have permissionless protocols that have intelligent defense. This is what we are building with SHIELD and invite everyone to join to make SHIELD industry-wide.

text:
Tempo was at @Sibos this week, meeting with institutions to bring real-world payments and settlement onchain.

Here are the key takeaways from the team:

- @sytaylor: This was the year of tokenization. From the opening keynote, to the show floor to even the standards talk.
- @ninadnirgudkar: The cash leg is the most important unit of any financial transaction. Moving it well across types of cash, like stablecoins or deposits, and for use cases, from payments to margin, is the key to unlocking onchain markets at scale!
- @borjaneira_ : Stablecoins and Tokenized Deposits will coexist: tokenized deposits will streamline existing institutional corridors, while stablecoins will extend liquidity to every corner of the global economy.
- @malleshpai: Tokenization, stablecoins and tokenized deposits went from side-stage to center-stage this year, and the conversation has shifted from PoCs to production. Institutions are now asking which rails are easy to integrate and can actually handle real workloads.
- @jevgenijs: The key for institutions is using existing standards to move money, because they already solve some of the hardest problems in finance. Leveraging standards like ISO20022 with new forms of money, like stablecoins, will be the catalyst to get banks onchain.

text:
.@HackenClub ran its AI auditor against a live Daml smart contract on Canton, surfacing findings on authority, validation, and consent risk.

The session, run alongside @NODERS_TEAM, walked through a live contract step-by-step.

A few key takeaways from the session below.
author: CantonNetwork
quoted_text:
What did the AI Auditor find in the Daml smart contract? 4 takeaways for @CantonNetwork builders from yesterday’s session with @NODERS_TEAM ↓ 

• Łukasz Wolski, Technical Lead, Hacken: “Canton removes reentrancy, gas, and delegatecall. The risk moves to different places: authority, validation, visibility, and state. None of these things produce a compiler error.”

• Kornel Światłowski, Smart Contract Auditor, Hacken: “When you put a house as collateral, the cash is supposed to be released only after both sides sign the contract. In this case, one person signed the contract, and the same person signed it again. The owner of the house cannot accept or decline the offer. The loan is created without his or her acceptance.”

• Ales, CPO, @NODERS_TEAM: “In lending, the counterparty is exactly who has a motivation to close a loan early. Who gets to declare a write-off is a business decision, not something any party to the contract should be able to trigger. How should teams think about insider risk from their own counterparties?”

• Farrukh Odinaev, Solutions Engineer, Hacken: “In our tests, when we tried to reduce false positives, we found an inverse correlation with the findings reported. The more you want to lower false positives, the fewer findings you get. You make your net too narrow, and it stops catching all important bugs.”

Watch Hacken’s Daml AI Auditor in action, followed by the findings review: https://t.co/gYYknRdBRb

text: Three months, two AI agents, and 5 million lines of Lean code later, delighted our classification of all order-6 semigroups is heading to MATH-AI@NeurIPS 2026!
author: nasqret
quoted_text:
Major announcement in mathematical formalization!

Finally, after 3 months of very intensive, nonstop work by several AI agents (Codex and Claude Code), we have settled a classification of ALL 15,973 semigroups of order 6. Every one of the 15,969 that has a finite basis now has it written down explicitly, and the remaining 4 are proved to have none at all.

The whole list of bases is produced for the first time in history. Until now, for most of these semigroups, mathematicians only knew that a basis exists; nobody had ever written one down. The formalization in Lean, orchestrated with a multi-agent approach, reached more than 5 MILLION lines of verified Lean code, one of the largest auto-formalization projects to date. 

It's been an amazing joint work with @JanotaMikolas and @Jan_Hula, accompanied by senior experts in semigroup theory, João Araújo and Edmond W. H. Lee.

Our paper describing this project, "Proving at Scale for Universal Algebra", has been accepted at the MATH-AI workshop, NeurIPS 2026!

When we launched this project, we were a bit pessimistic: producing proofs for 15,973 semigroups seemed out of scope for the current technology. But with a careful setup (agents communicating through a mailbox we arranged, orchestrating the effort with a custom method of bootstrapping and auto-research), it has finally come to the finish line. The last 390 semigroups took 23 more days. The very last one needed a whole structural analysis before its proof could even be written.

text:
NEAR AI has claimed first place on the Lean Eval v1 leaderboard.

Lean Eval v1 is an active benchmark maintained by Lean FRO that contains extremely hard formalization problems. We reached first place despite joining the competition just four weeks ago, a full month later than other top participants.

NEAR is very heavily investing in formal verification efforts. Our ultimate goal is to formally prove the protocol and all the core contracts, and to provide a practical tool for others to formally verify their contracts in a fast and affordable way.

The system that enabled us to claim first place is almost entirely powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and thus is (a) extremely cheap, and (b) has no dependencies on third parties because the model is open weight.

When it comes to formally verifying software, the approach boils down to three pillars:
1. Representing the program in a way that can be reasoned about;
2. Expressing the properties that we desire to prove;
3. Coming up with a proof and formalizing it in Lean.

Until recently, step (3) was prohibitively expensive for practical use at scale. With the system that we used for Lean Eval, we now have it solved. Stay tuned for updates on how we apply it in practice to formally verify NEAR contracts.

text:
Major announcement in mathematical formalization!

Finally, after 3 months of very intensive, nonstop work by several AI agents (Codex and Claude Code), we have settled a classification of ALL 15,973 semigroups of order 6. Every one of the 15,969 that has a finite basis now has it written down explicitly, and the remaining 4 are proved to have none at all.

The whole list of bases is produced for the first time in history. Until now, for most of these semigroups, mathematicians only knew that a basis exists; nobody had ever written one down. The formalization in Lean, orchestrated with a multi-agent approach, reached more than 5 MILLION lines of verified Lean code, one of the largest auto-formalization projects to date. 

It's been an amazing joint work with @JanotaMikolas and @Jan_Hula, accompanied by senior experts in semigroup theory, João Araújo and Edmond W. H. Lee.

Our paper describing this project, "Proving at Scale for Universal Algebra", has been accepted at the MATH-AI workshop, NeurIPS 2026!

When we launched this project, we were a bit pessimistic: producing proofs for 15,973 semigroups seemed out of scope for the current technology. But with a careful setup (agents communicating through a mailbox we arranged, orchestrating the effort with a custom method of bootstrapping and auto-research), it has finally come to the finish line. The last 390 semigroups took 23 more days. The very last one needed a whole structural analysis before its proof could even be written.

Tempo was at @Sibos this week, meeting with institutions to bring real-world payments and settlement onchain.

Here are the key takeaways from the team:

- @sytaylor: This was the year of tokenization. From the opening keynote, to the show floor to even the standards talk.
- @ninadnirgudkar: The cash leg is the most important unit of any financial transaction. Moving it well across types of cash, like stablecoins or deposits, and for use cases, from payments to margin, is the key to unlocking onchain markets at scale!
- @borjaneira_ : Stablecoins and Tokenized Deposits will coexist: tokenized deposits will streamline existing institutional corridors, while stablecoins will extend liquidity to every corner of the global economy.
- @malleshpai: Tokenization, stablecoins and tokenized deposits went from side-stage to center-stage this year, and the conversation has shifted from PoCs to production. Institutions are now asking which rails are easy to integrate and can actually handle real workloads.
- @jevgenijs: The key for institutions is using existing standards to move money, because they already solve some of the hardest problems in finance. Leveraging standards like ISO20022 with new forms of money, like stablecoins, will be the catalyst to get banks onchain.

text:
Crypto has no shortage of tokens.

What it still needs more of are reasons to actually use them.

Trading and DeFi proved that financial activity works onchain. Prediction markets proved people will put money behind a view. Gaming showed another direction entirely.

But these things still mostly live in their own boxes.

That’s the part I find interesting.

Why can’t one onchain economy sit underneath completely different experiences? One day you’re competing in a market arena, another day you’re playing someone live, another day you’re watching and participating from the sidelines.

That’s basically where KRYVAN came from.

And Solana made sense for it. If you want lots of small interactions between real users, you need speed and fees low enough that using the product doesn’t become the annoying part of the product.

$KRVN is being built as the layer running through those experiences, not as something we launch first and then spend the next year trying to invent a use for.

Build the experiences.

If people actually enjoy using them, the onchain economy has a reason to exist.

That’s the bet.

#Solana #KRYVAN #BuildInPublic

NEAR AI is now #1 on Lean Eval v1, Lean FRO's active benchmark of extremely hard formalization problems.

The system runs almost entirely on open-weight DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, so it's low cost and has no third-party model dependency.

author: NEARProtocol
quoted_text:
NEAR AI has claimed first place on the Lean Eval v1 leaderboard.

Lean Eval v1 is an active benchmark maintained by Lean FRO that contains extremely hard formalization problems. We reached first place despite joining the competition just four weeks ago, a full month later than other top participants.

NEAR is very heavily investing in formal verification efforts. Our ultimate goal is to formally prove the protocol and all the core contracts, and to provide a practical tool for others to formally verify their contracts in a fast and affordable way.

The system that enabled us to claim first place is almost entirely powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and thus is (a) extremely cheap, and (b) has no dependencies on third parties because the model is open weight.

When it comes to formally verifying software, the approach boils down to three pillars:
1. Representing the program in a way that can be reasoned about;
2. Expressing the properties that we desire to prove;
3. Coming up with a proof and formalizing it in Lean.

Until recently, step (3) was prohibitively expensive for practical use at scale. With the system that we used for Lean Eval, we now have it solved. Stay tuned for updates on how we apply it in practice to formally verify NEAR contracts.

text:
the agentic trading stack is taking shape faster than i expected

after looking across the eco, i think intelligence is now the main bottleneck

the infra already exists:

- agent wallets from @privy_io, @coinbase and others
- identity standards such as ERC-8004 and ERC-8183
- institutional market data through @PythNetwork Pro AI
- liquidity from @HyperliquidX, @OndoPerps and soon @LayerZero_Core's ATLAS
- MCP access through platforms such as @RobinhoodApp 

agents can already access data, hold funds and execute trades under predefined controls

but access does not make an agent a good trader

when Robinhood opened its markets through MCP, @vladtenev noted that agents would often refuse to trade

his explanation = current models are trained heavily on coding data, but have very little trading data

trading requires more than generating a bullish or bearish answer

the agent needs to:
- understand the market regime
- find and validate setups
- challenge the original thesis
- size risk correctly
- monitor positions continuously
- review previous trades and improve

then @get_truenorth caught my attention

it's building what it calls an agentic brokerage, combining the intelligence layer with direct market access

on the intelligence side, it pulls data from 40+ real-time sources

including CoinGecko, DeFiLlama, Hyperliquid, Polymarket, Deribit and several CEXs

humans cannot continuously monitor every market, macro release, funding shift and position but agents can

i think most value in agentic trading will concentrate in 2 layers:

[1] Intelligence that consistently improves decisions

[2] Liquidity infra that provides reliable execution

products that control neither may struggle to retain value

i’m watching which platforms can turn that access into measurable trading performance
