Blast will be shutting down.

We launched Blast with the goal of building a self-sustaining chain for users and developers. Unfortunately, the economics of operating the chain no longer make sense: the ongoing costs of maintaining Blast exceed the revenue generated by the L2, and we do not see a credible path to making the chain economically sustainable.

As a result, we've made the difficult decision to wind Blast down.

We're sorry to the users and developers who believed in Blast, built on it, and supported the ecosystem. Our priority now is making the shutdown as smooth and safe as possible.

We're asking all users to withdraw their assets from Blast to Ethereum mainnet, including any balances held in the Blast PWA.

To make this easier, we will be reducing the withdrawal delay to 24 hours.

As part of the shutdown process, we'll first begin withdrawing Blast's Lido assets. This process is expected to take approximately one week. During this period, withdrawals will temporarily be unavailable, even after the withdrawal delay is reduced to 24 hours.

Once that process is complete, withdrawals will resume with the new 24-hour delay.

Users will have until October 26, 2026 to withdraw through the normal Blast interface.

After October 26, assets will remain withdrawable, but users will need to interact directly with the Blast bridge contracts on Ethereum L1. We'll publish detailed instructions before then.

We strongly encourage everyone to withdraw their assets to Ethereum mainnet before October 26.

🚨 Derive now wants to allocate half of the fees generated to buying back ethereum:0xb1d1eae60eea9525032a6dcb4c1ce336a1de71be 

The DAO of @DeriveXYZ, the first on-chain options DEX, has submitted a new governance proposal to raise the share of protocol fees allocated to buybacks from 35% to 50%.

This idea is not new. In May 2025, a community member had already proposed increasing this share to 80%, but it did not go through.

Eventually, last April, the DAO approved the move from 25% to 35%, while reducing staking emissions from 250,000 to 100,000 DRV per week.

If a similar proposal is coming back today, it is mainly because the context is no longer the same. After a rather quiet 2025, the fees generated by the protocol have risen sharply since March, with several weeks above $200,000. 

Over the last 30 days, Derive has posted $665 000 in fees generated, or around 8 million annualized.

Taking this information into account (optimistic estimates), here is what the move to 50% would change:

◻️ Buybacks would go from around 2.8 to 4 million dollars per year.

◻️ At the current price, this represents nearly 208,000 DRV bought back each week, compared with 150-190 000 currently.

◻️In return, the share left to the security module and market-maker rebates would go from around 5.2 to 4 million dollars per year.

The important point to know is that, on average, buybacks already cover each week's emissions. Derive distributes 150,000 DRV per week, including 100,000 for stakers and 50,000 for trading incentives. 

With a 50% allocation, the protocol would therefore buy back significantly more tokens than it emits, and the gap would widen as fees grow.

The other point to keep in mind is that this is a simple buyback, with no burn. The 27.8 million ethereum:0xb1d1eae60eea9525032a6dcb4c1ce336a1de71be bought back so far are placed in the DAO's treasury. 

This proposal paves the way for a new economic model, where buybacks would be used to fund staker rewards, in order to allow the protocol to stop weekly token emissions.

On our side, we believe the proposal has a good chance of passing, all the more so as the timing is largely favorable. 

The token has gained 170% in one month, Derive is today by far the leader in on-chain options, and V3 arrives on October 6.

It remains to be seen what holders really stand to gain if the bought-back tokens end up redistributed to stakers rather than being burned.

Find our full analysis in the Alpha Feed dedicated to Derive👇

text:
Here’s my 5 key KBW takeaways: 

1) AI overkill: So many teams have pivoted to AI that it’s becoming a visibly overplayed buzzword. In some cases, it feels like a last lifeline attempt to find PMF. My read is that far fewer are actually building something differentiated or meaningful on this front so tread lightly with people who are “building” here. 
2) Founder shift: A few VCs shared that a growing number of new founders aren’t even positioning themselves as “crypto” founders in pitch decks or hackathons. They’re still using the underlying blockchain technology but are building businesses in other categories like AI, fintech, financial infrastructure, etc. and letting the application define the company (ex a payments business) rather than the underlying rails (ex a stablecoin driven business.)
3) Institutional conversations: Some well-connected executives building on the convergence of TradFi / DeFi told me that the crypto community has broadly misunderstood where banks and larger institutions actually stand. Their view is that many institutions already see this technology as inevitable and are primarily thinking about how to use it to make more money, rather than whether they should participate at all. 
4) Hot topics: 24/7 trading, perps and related products are major accelerants and areas for growth. They’re coming, if they aren’t already here. Some teams I spoke with think trading volume on this front will always be led by DEXs given the first mover advantage. But I wouldn’t count out mainstream exchanges long term though as it’s still early days. Separately, there was less talk about tokenization, which was surprising, but tokenized equities specifically kept coming up in conversation, unsurprisingly.
5) Who was actually there? I saw a number of high-profile attendees from U.S. and Korean companies, as well as government roles, which spoke to the caliber of people in the room and the continued interest in accessing this market. On the conference floor, traders were clearly a major category from attendees, which speaks to the retail interest. I also suspect more Korean enterprises are exploring this privately than is visible publicly, given the level of interest and attendance as well. 

Disclaimer: pic is from last year’s conference :)

抱歉，我之前误解了你的说法，为此向你致歉。你的观点很有道理，我也明白了你的顾虑所在。

正如之前提到的，我们正在逐步进行升级；你说得对的一点是，目前的销毁率确实尚未调整，且“领取”（claim）环节也尚未实现完全去中心化。

我不是中国人，所以没能通读全部内容，当时误以为你只是担心回购销毁的速度太慢。

我们一直在调整这套系统，目前我正在链上升级合约，因此你会看到资金流向发生变化。新的回购机制设计为：每7天执行一次“领取”操作，随后在接下来的7天内将领取的资金全部用于回购销毁，并循环往复。我认为这种方式能确保建立一个良好且可持续的回购销毁机制。

对于我之前的仓促回复以及指责你做出错误推断一事，我再次表示歉意。当时我没有读完所有细节，便想当然地将其归类为“大家都在关心的那个我们正在解决的问题”之中。

希望这能消除误会，再次向你致歉。我不介意自己出错，也认为如果我确实错了，理应指出来。
